The Adventures of Book 9: Polyphemus the Cyclops

In Book 9, Odysseus narrates one of the most famous episodes in all of ancient literature: the encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus and twelve chosen companions enter the enormous cave of Polyphemus — a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead — in hopes of receiving the gift of xenia, the code of hospitality that any Greek host owed a stranger. Instead, Polyphemus seals the cave with a massive boulder, seizes two of the men and eats them raw. He will do the same each morning and evening for as long as Odysseus remains his prisoner.

Odysseus’s first instinct is to stab Polyphemus in his sleep, but he quickly realises that would be fatal: only the giant can move the boulder that blocks the entrance. This moment shows the essential quality that distinguishes Odysseus from other heroes — his metis, or cunning intelligence. Brute force would kill him. He must think.

Key Fact

Odysseus’s escape plan has four stages: he finds a wooden stake in the cave, sharpens and hardens its tip in the fire, gets Polyphemus drunk on wine, blinds him by driving the stake into his eye, and then hides his men (and himself) beneath the giant’s rams as they leave the cave in the morning — since Polyphemus runs his hands over the backs of the sheep but does not check their undersides.

The ‘Nobody’ Trick

When Polyphemus, reeling from the wine, asks Odysseus his name so he can give him a “gift” of xenia in return, Odysseus tells him his name is “Nobody” — Outis in Greek. When Odysseus drives the stake into Polyphemus’s eye and the giant screams in agony, the neighbouring Cyclopes come to the entrance of the cave and ask what the matter is. “Nobody is killing me,” roars Polyphemus. The others conclude he must be ill and go away. The trick is a masterstroke of wordplay and deception: in the oblique grammatical forms Polyphemus uses when reporting his pain, mē tis (no one) becomes indistinguishable from mētis (cunning intelligence), creating a layered pun that quietly signals the quality that has defeated him.

However, Odysseus’s cunning is shadowed by a fatal flaw: excessive pride. As his ships pull safely away from the island, Odysseus cannot resist taunting Polyphemus and — crucially — revealing his real name. He shouts that it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, from Ithaca, who blinded him. Polyphemus calls on his father, the sea-god Poseidon, to curse Odysseus. This moment plants the seed of every subsequent delay in Odysseus’s return: Poseidon will make the sea his enemy for the rest of the poem.

Polyphemus embodies everything that is the opposite of civilised Greek society. He does not farm the land — he lives entirely off his flock. He has no concept of the gods or of xenia: when Odysseus invokes Zeus as the protector of guests, Polyphemus dismisses the gods entirely, saying the Cyclopes are stronger than any immortal. He lives alone, with no community or law. He eats his guests rather than feeding them.

Homer signals his barbarism through precise descriptive details. His cave is enormous but messy and unstructured — milk pails and cheese are stored without order; pens of lambs are organised only by age. He sits among his flocks like a man among animals. In contrast, Odysseus and his men, for all their fear, maintain their civilised behaviour, discussing options and following a plan. The contrast between Odysseus’s intelligence and the Cyclops’s brute size is the central drama of the episode.

Book 10: The Witch Circe

In Book 10, after further adventures, Odysseus’s ships arrive at the island of Aeaea, home of the goddess-witch Circe. Odysseus sends a scouting party — half his men — to explore the island. They find a palace in a woodland clearing, surrounded by wolves and lions, which are in fact men Circe has already transformed. Circe invites the men in and serves them a feast laced with a drug. When they eat, she strikes them with her wand and turns them into pigs. Only one man, Eurylochus, escapes because he hangs back, suspicious.

Odysseus sets out alone to rescue his men. On the way, the god Hermes meets him in the form of a young man and gives him the herb moly — a white flower with a black root — which will counteract Circe’s magic. He also instructs Odysseus to rush at Circe with his sword when she tries to transform him. Circe, astonished that her magic has failed, recognises Odysseus and surrenders. She restores his crew, and Odysseus and his men stay on the island for a year, feasting with Circe as their willing host.

Key Fact

Hermes gives Odysseus the herb moly to protect him from Circe’s magic. When Circe’s drug fails to transform Odysseus, she recognises him as the man foretold by Hermes. He forces her to swear an oath not to harm him, and she restores his men. This episode is significant because Circe, unlike Polyphemus, ultimately fulfils the obligations of xenia: she feeds, hosts and eventually helps Odysseus.

Circe is one of Homer’s most interesting characters. She begins the episode as a dangerous, magical predator who destroys men without warning. But once Odysseus resists her magic and confronts her directly, she transforms into a generous and knowledgeable host. She provides food, rest and, crucially, information: it is Circe who tells Odysseus he must travel to the Underworld to consult the dead prophet Teiresias before he can find his way home.

This transformation from threat to helper reveals something about Odysseus’s ability to bring order out of chaos through force of will and intelligence. It also raises the question of how Homer portrays powerful women. Circe has divine power, knowledge and authority that most of the male characters in the poem lack. Yet she ultimately places herself in service to Odysseus’s mission. The tension between her power and her submission to Odysseus reflects the poem’s broader interest in what makes a man truly dominant.

The Crew of Odysseus

In both episodes, the crew of Odysseus plays a crucial role — and not always a heroic one. In the Cyclops episode, it is one of Odysseus’s men who spots the cheese and lambs in Polyphemus’s cave and urges him to take them, rather than leaving as caution demanded. In Book 10, the crew’s curiosity and recklessness lead directly to their transformation into pigs. Homer’s point is consistent: Odysseus’s men lack their leader’s self-restraint and sophrosyne — the quality of knowing one’s limits. The men are brave and loyal, but they cannot resist the temptations placed in their way, and this failure will ultimately destroy them.

before.content_html:
The Return to Ithaca: Disguise and Deception

When Odysseus finally reaches Ithaca in Book 13, the goddess Athena disguises him as an old beggar. This disguise is essential to his plan: Ithaca is filled with over a hundred suitors who have taken over his palace, are consuming his wealth and are competing to marry his wife Penelope. If Odysseus is recognised too soon, he will be killed before he can prepare. The disguise is one of the most sustained and elaborate acts of deception in the poem, and it lasts through Books 13 to 22.

The theme of disguise and recognition is one of the Odyssey’s most powerful structural devices. Homer builds intense dramatic irony by allowing the audience to know what the characters in the poem do not: the ragged beggar shuffling through the halls of his own palace is the great king Odysseus. This gap between what the audience knows and what the suitors assume — that they are safe, that Odysseus is dead, that they may treat a helpless beggar with contempt — makes their eventual destruction feel both inevitable and just.

Book 19: Penelope and the Recognition by Eurycleia

In Book 19, still in his beggar’s disguise, Odysseus has a long, remarkable conversation with Penelope. She does not know she is speaking to her husband. She tells the “stranger” about her famous trick: she has been weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus’s father Laertes and has promised to choose a new husband when it is finished. Every night she unpicks the weaving she has done during the day, buying herself years of time. This deception is a mirror of Odysseus’s own resourcefulness — husband and wife are revealed to be perfectly matched in their use of cunning to protect what matters most to them.

The recognition scene that follows is both touching and tense. Penelope calls for the old nurse Eurycleia to wash the beggar’s feet — an act of hospitality appropriate for a guest. As Eurycleia washes his legs, her hands find a scar on his thigh. The poem pauses the action entirely to tell the story of how Odysseus received the scar as a young man, hunting a boar on Mount Parnassus with his grandfather Autolycus. This long digression — a retardation technique, not the anagnorisis itself — is a deliberate slowing of the pace that builds the dramatic tension almost unbearably. The anagnorisis comes immediately after: the moment Eurycleia’s hands find the scar and she realises the beggar is Odysseus.

Eurycleia gasps and looks up. Odysseus grabs her throat and silences her with a warning: no one must know. She agrees. This is the first human recognition in the palace, and it confirms for the audience what Odysseus has known all along — that there are loyal people in Ithaca waiting for his return, and that his plan can succeed.

Key Fact

Penelope’s weaving deception is her equivalent of Odysseus’s cunning: she weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicks it by night, delaying her choice of a husband for years. The parallel between husband and wife — both using deception to hold off those who would take what is theirs — is one of Homer’s most deliberate structural echoes.

Book 21: The Contest of the Bow

In Book 21, Penelope announces a contest to decide who she will marry: any man who can string Odysseus’s great bow and shoot an arrow through the sockets of twelve axe-heads in a row may have her hand. The great bow of Odysseus, given to him long ago by the hero Iphitus, is an object of enormous symbolic importance. It is kept under lock and key and has not been used since he left for Troy. To string it requires enormous strength and skill — the kind that only its owner possesses.

One by one, the suitors try and fail to string the bow. The wood is seasoned and stiff; the string requires a technique that none of them can master. The contest grinds to a humiliating halt. Then Odysseus, still in his beggar’s disguise, asks to be allowed to try. The suitors mock him furiously. Penelope supports his right to attempt it. Odysseus strings the bow with casual ease — “as a skilled musician strings a lyre,” as Homer says in one of his most elegant extended similes — and shoots cleanly through all twelve axe-heads without rising from his stool.

The homecoming books contrast loyal and disloyal servants carefully. The swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius remain loyal to Odysseus throughout: they refuse to side with the suitors, treat the disguised beggar with xenia, and are entrusted with a role in the final battle. Eurycleia recognises Odysseus and keeps his secret.

In contrast, twelve maidservants have slept with the suitors and sided against Penelope. The goatherd Melanthius has actively helped the suitors and insults Odysseus even when disguised. After the slaughter of the suitors, these disloyal servants are punished: the maidservants are forced to clean up the bodies before being hanged in the courtyard, and Melanthius is mutilated. The poem’s treatment of these characters reflects a worldview in which loyalty to a rightful lord is a supreme virtue, and its betrayal demands the harshest punishment.

Book 22: The Slaughter of the Suitors

The moment after Odysseus strings the bow is the pivot of the whole poem. He turns, shoots the leading suitor Antinous through the throat, and announces himself: “You thought I would never come home from Troy. You have been wasting my household, violating my maidservants, and seeking to take my wife while I still lived. Dogs — you never feared the gods who rule the spacious heaven, or the anger of men to come. Your day of reckoning has arrived.” The battle that follows is swift and brutal. Odysseus and three loyal helpers — his son Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius — kill all the suitors in the great hall.

The massacre is presented by Homer as an act of dike — justice — rather than mere revenge. The suitors have violated the sacred rules of xenia by abusing their host’s hospitality for years. They have dishonoured Penelope, threatened Telemachus and wasted Odysseus’s wealth. The gods, particularly Zeus, have sanctioned the punishment. Athena appears in the hall to tip the balance at a critical moment, showing that divine approval stamps the act as righteous.

Key Fact

The suitors are killed by Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius in Book 22. Homer frames the slaughter as divinely sanctioned justice: the suitors violated xenia, threatened the rightful king’s household, and dishonoured the gods. Athena’s presence in the hall confirms divine approval.

The scale of the killing in Book 22 — over a hundred young noblemen murdered in the great hall — can shock modern readers. Homer is not naive about this: the families of the suitors object in Book 24 and Odysseus faces a further threat of civil war. Yet throughout the poem Homer has built a careful moral case. The suitors were repeatedly warned. The gods disapproved. Odysseus returned precisely in time to prevent Penelope being forced into a new marriage. The contest of the bow — Penelope’s idea, not Odysseus’s — gave the suitors every opportunity to redeem themselves if any had the strength to string the bow.

The poem’s final moral position is that the gods uphold justice, and that those who violate the sacred laws of xenia and respect for a rightful king will be punished. Odysseus is the instrument of that punishment. Whether readers find this satisfying or disturbing often depends on whether they share Homer’s worldview — and that difference of response is itself worth discussing in a good exam answer.

The Role of the Gods in the Odyssey

The gods are not background figures in the Odyssey — they are active participants in the story, intervening at crucial moments to help or hinder the mortals they favour or resent. Homer opens the poem in a divine assembly: Zeus reflects that mortals blame the gods for their suffering, when in fact their own recklessness is usually the cause. This opening sets up the poem’s moral framework. The gods are not arbitrary or capricious in Homer’s version — they punish those who deserve it and reward those who honour them properly.

The two most important divine figures in the Odyssey stand in direct opposition to each other. Athena is Odysseus’s protector. She engineers his release from Calypso’s island by appealing to Zeus, guides Telemachus on his journey, gives Odysseus his beggar’s disguise, and intervenes in the battle of Book 22. Poseidon is Odysseus’s enemy. After Odysseus blinds his son Polyphemus, Poseidon does everything he can to prevent the homecoming — destroying ships, stranding the hero on distant islands, and stirring up deadly storms.

Key Fact

Athena (protector) and Poseidon (enemy) represent the two opposing divine forces in the Odyssey. The tension between them drives the structure of the poem: every time Poseidon obstructs Odysseus, Athena finds a way to help him forward. The poem suggests that Odysseus’s eventual success is divinely sanctioned — justice, as well as intelligence, is on his side.

Fate, Free Will and Divine Justice

A central question in the Odyssey is how much of what happens to characters is their own fault, and how much is the will of the gods. Zeus’s speech at the opening of the poem signals Homer’s position: mortals suffer when they act recklessly against divine warnings. Odysseus’s crew are warned not to eat the cattle of Helios; they eat them anyway and are destroyed. The suitors are given multiple warnings; they persist in their behaviour and are killed. Odysseus himself earns Poseidon’s enmity through his own pride.

Yet the gods are not neutral. Athena actively promotes Odysseus’s cause, and her intervention in Book 22 — appearing in the hall to tip the balance — shows that divine favour is not merely passive approval but direct action. The poem holds both ideas simultaneously: mortals are responsible for their own choices, and the gods shape the world those choices are made in. This is not a contradiction but a coherent worldview in which moral responsibility and divine authority coexist.

Xenia — guest-friendship — is arguably the most important value in the Odyssey. The code required a host to welcome any stranger with food and shelter before asking who they were or why they had come. It required guests to behave respectfully and not overstay their welcome. The whole system was protected by Zeus in his role as Zeus Xenios — protector of guests and strangers. Violation of xenia was a religious offence, not just a social one.

The poem is full of xenia encounters, and each one tests whether the code is being followed. The Phaeacians in Books 7 and 8 are model hosts: they entertain Odysseus lavishly, give him gifts, and eventually escort him home in their magical ships. The suitors in Ithaca are the counter-example: they have been “guests” in Odysseus’s hall for years, but they consume his wealth, harass his wife, threaten his son and abuse the real guests — most notably, the disguised Odysseus himself. Their violation of xenia is not just rude; it is impious. This is why their deaths are presented as divine justice rather than mere revenge.

Good Hosts and Bad Hosts in the Odyssey

One of the most consistent ways Homer builds his moral universe is by measuring each character and community against the standard of xenia. The contrast between good and bad hosts is a structural principle of the poem. Polyphemus is the worst possible host: he eats his guests instead of feeding them, dismisses the gods who protect xenia, and has no concept of the reciprocal obligation that defines civilised behaviour. The Phaeacians, by contrast, bring xenia to near-perfection: they ask no questions, provide lavish entertainment, allow Odysseus to tell his own story, and escort him home with gifts.

Circe begins as a hostile and dangerous host but is transformed by Odysseus’s resistance into a genuine one. She provides a year of hospitality, restores his crew, and gives him essential information. This progression — from failed xenia to fulfilled xenia — mirrors the arc of the whole poem: disorder being brought back to order, the world resetting around the proper code of behaviour.

Key Fact

The Phaeacians are the model hosts of the Odyssey: they entertain Odysseus without questions, hold games in his honour, allow him to narrate his adventures (Books 9–12), and eventually carry him home. This perfect xenia is deliberately contrasted with the suitors in Ithaca, who have turned the rules of hospitality entirely upside down.

Penelope: Host, Wife and Queen

Penelope is one of the most complex female characters in ancient literature. She is simultaneously a faithful wife (waiting twenty years for Odysseus), a resourceful strategist (the weaving trick, the bow contest), and a host who maintains the laws of xenia even under enormous pressure. When the disguised Odysseus arrives at the palace, it is Penelope who insists he be welcomed and treated according to the code — she orders Eurycleia to wash his feet and provides him with a bed, even as the suitors mock him.

Penelope’s intelligence mirrors Odysseus’s. The weaving trick shows she can use deception to protect what she values, just as Odysseus does. The bow contest in Book 21 is entirely her idea — Odysseus did not plan it. By setting the contest, she creates the mechanism for Odysseus’s revelation and the suitors’ destruction, though the poem is ambiguous about whether she consciously intends this or acts on instinct. This ambiguity makes her fascinating: she may be even more complicit in the plan than Homer openly states.

Telemachus begins the Odyssey as a boy unable to challenge the suitors. By Books 21 and 22, he stands beside his father and kills men in battle. His development — from passive youth to active hero — is one of the poem’s most carefully traced arcs. Athena appears to him in disguise at the start of the poem, encouraging him to seek news of his father and to start behaving like a prince. This divine push sets him on his journey.

Telemachus’s role in the homecoming is not merely that of a helper: he is Odysseus’s heir and the future of Ithaca. When Odysseus trusts him with the knowledge of his identity, it is because Telemachus has shown he is worthy. His willingness to fight alongside his father rather than hiding shows that the next generation of Ithaca’s ruling house is as capable as the last. The Odyssey is not just a story about one man returning home — it is about the restoration of a household and a dynasty.

Women and Men in the Homeric World

The Odyssey contains some of the most memorable female characters in ancient literature: Penelope, Circe, Calypso, the Phaeacian princess Nausicaa. This is not accidental. The poem’s central drama — the household of Ithaca under threat — is also a drama about the proper ordering of gender roles in Homer’s world. Penelope is celebrated precisely because she remains faithful and uses her intelligence in service of her husband’s return. Circe and Calypso are dangerous precisely because they represent the temptation to abandon that domestic world: Circe’s island (for a year) and Calypso’s (for seven years) are places where Odysseus forgets, temporarily, who he is. The poem consistently values homecoming over staying, and domestic loyalty over divine pleasure.
